story_type: retired frigate sunk by live fire in a multinational sinking exercise
hook: Three navies opened fire on this frigate. That was the plan.
narration: Ships and planes from three navies opened fire on this frigate, and it was all planned.
It was the USS Crommelin, a decommissioned Navy frigate, fifty-five nautical miles north of Kauai.
In July twenty sixteen, during the RIMPAC exercise, it became a live target in a sinking exercise.
Ships from Canada, New Zealand and the United States fired on it, along with U.S. and Australian aircraft.
The littoral combat ship USS Coronado fired a Harpoon missile, the first ever from its class of ship.
Before a hulk is sunk like this, crews strip out PCBs, mercury and other hazards under an E P A permit.
The rules also say it must go down at least fifty nautical miles from land, in water at least six thousand feet deep.
outcome: The Crommelin was sunk north of Kauai, in water fifteen thousand feet deep.
title: Three navies open fire on a frigate
description:
On July 19, 2016, ships and aircraft taking part in the RIMPAC exercise sank the decommissioned frigate USS Crommelin with live fire 55 nautical miles north of Kauai, Hawaii.

question_comment: Should old warships be sunk for practice or turned into museums?

extra_sources.excerpt: Navy News Service release NNS160720-13, Commander, U.S. 3rd Fleet, July 20, 2016: USS Crommelin (FFG 37) sunk by live fire from HMCS Calgary, HMNZS Te Kaha, USS Coronado and U.S. and Australian aircraft, July 19, 55 nautical miles north of Kauai in water 15,000 feet deep; first time that the U.S. Independence-variant littoral combat ship successfully fired a harpoon missile; hulk cleaned of PCBs and mercury-containing materials under an EPA general permit; SINKEX hulks must sink in at least 1,000 fathoms (6,000 feet) of water and at least 50 nautical miles from land.
